ideas.title: Droop-governed risk parity with a 4%-per-day ramp limit and a 10% spinning-reserve cash floor
ideas.sketch: The base target is inverse-volatility risk parity across all 10 ETFs (63-day volatility of daily close-to-close returns), and the controller acts on the drawdown of the strategy's own NAV from its trailing 252-day peak, which plays the role of the grid's frequency deviation. Target gross exposure follows a droop law with a deadband, E_t = clip(0.90 - 8*(DD_t - 0.04), 0.25, 0.90): there is no action inside a 4% drawdown, each further 1% of drawdown removes 8% of exposure, and the 0.25 floor is reached at about 12% DD, which leaves roughly 8 points of headroom to the 20% limit. The permanent 10% cash is the spinning reserve; it makes re-risking after a V-shaped recovery (as in 2020) possible without selling anything. Execution is ramp-limited: each trading day the portfolio moves toward target along the straight-line gap vector, scaled so one-way turnover sum|dw|/2 is at most 4%. Five days times 4% bounds weekly turnover at 20% by construction, and because the volatility estimates change with every close, the gap is almost surely nonzero, so trades happen on every day. To make that guarantee hold by rule rather than by probability, any Monday, Wednesday or Friday whose computed trade is below 0.05% instead makes a 0.05% 'reserve test' transfer between cash and the most-underweight ETF. The transfer is fairly literal (droop is essentially a drawdown-keyed CPPI, which is not new), but the ramp cap is a genuine contribution: it makes the turnover and frequency gates the control law itself instead of clipping bolted on. The honest weakness is that a 64-point de-risk takes about 16 trading days, so a 2020-style fall of about 10% in three weeks is only partly absorbed. My estimate is a worst case of about 13-16% DD and net growth of about 4.5-5.5% a year, taking unlevered risk-parity returns less the reserve drag and less than 10 bp of cost.

ideas.title: N-1 contingency reserve: size exposure so losing the largest asset-class 'generator' cannot breach the drawdown limit, with asymmetric primary/secondary ramps
ideas.sketch: The ETFs are grouped into three 'generating units', Equity (US large, US small, developed ex-US, EM, REITs), Duration (7-10y Treasuries, TIPS, IG credit) and Real (gold, broad commodities), and each unit gets equal risk contribution at the cluster level (63-day covariance of cluster returns); within a cluster the weights are inverse volatility, halved for any ETF whose close is below its 200-day SMA. Each day the rule computes each cluster's contingency loss L_c, the 1st-percentile 10-day return over the trailing 1260 days, and a correlated-stress loss S_t = max_c(w_c*L_c) + 0.5*sum_{other c}(w_c*L_c), which transfers the grid's N-1 criterion (the largest unit trips while the others sag) to a correlated sell-off such as 2008 or 2022. Invested exposure is lambda_t = min(0.95, H_t/S_t), where H_t = 0.17 - DD_t is the remaining drawdown headroom (the 20% limit less a 3-point safety margin), so cash is exactly the reserve needed to survive the largest plausible contingency, never less than 5%. The primary response (cutting risk) is ramp-limited to 4% one-way per day, and the secondary response (AGC-like restoration of risk) to 2% per day. With five trading days, even the worst mix is at most 20% weekly turnover, and the slower upward ramp damps the whipsaw oscillations that a symmetric controller would produce. Trading on three or more days follows from the daily covariance, L_c and DD updates, backed by the same 0.05% reserve-test dither on Mon/Wed/Fri. The transfer is stronger than plain droop, because N-1 sizing gives an explicit, auditable worst-case argument addressed to correlated stress, and the diversification rubric is met by rule because no cluster carries more than a third of the risk. The main doubt is that L_c from a 5-year window can understate a new regime (for example, 2022 bond losses after 2017-2021 calm), which the 3-point margin only partly covers; my net growth estimate is about 4-5.5% a year.
